The third: it is the floor of the valley, and perhaps it refers to the dust raised from this place.

﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a gathering﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

The first: the gathering of the enemy, until the onslaught meets. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan.

The second: it is Muzdalifah, called a gathering (jamʿ) because the pilgrims gather there, and the raising of dust in the rush to Mina. This is the view of Makḥūl.

﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord﴾. Concerning al-kanūd (ungrateful) there are seven opinions:

The first: it means kafūr (disbelieving, ungrateful). This is the view of Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Jubayr, and from it comes the saying of al-Aʿshā:

"Renew for her [love], and she will renew for your union; indeed, she is ungrateful (kunud) to the union of the frequent visitor."

It is also said that al-kanūd is one who denies a little and does not give thanks for much.

The second: it is one who reproaches his Lord, mentioning calamities and forgetting blessings. This is the view of al-Ḥasan, and it is close to the first meaning.

The third: al-kanūd is one who denies the truth. It is said that Kindah was so named because it denied its father. Ibrāhīm ibn Zuhayr the poet said:

"Leave the miserly, if they are haughty and refuse, and the mention of the miserliness of a ungrateful beautiful woman."

The fourth: al-kanūd is the disobedient in the language of Kindah and Ḥaḍramawt. This was mentioned by Yaḥyā ibn Salām.

The fifth: it is the miserly in the language of Mālik ibn Kinānah. al-Kalbī said: al-kanūd in the language of Kindah and Ḥaḍramawt means the disobedient; in the language of Muḍar and Rabīʿah it means the ungrateful; and in the language of Mālik ibn Kinānah it means the miserly.

The sixth: he spends Allah's blessings on disobedience to Allah.

The seventh: what al-Qāsim narrated from Abū Umāmah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The kanūd is the one who beats his servant, eats alone, and withholds his gift." al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah. On this basis the oath falls upon all that preceded in the sūrah.

﴿And indeed, he is a witness to that﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

The first: Allah, exalted is He, is a witness to the disbelief of man. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The second: man is a witness against himself, because he is kanūd. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

﴿And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth﴾. This refers to man. Concerning al-khayr (wealth) here there are two opinions:

The first: it is wealth. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah.

The second: it is this world. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

It may also carry a third meaning: that al-khayr here is choice, and the meaning would be: indeed, he is intense in his love of his own choice.

Concerning His saying ﴿intense﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: he is intensely loving of good, and intensity of love is its strength and increase.

The second: he is stingy with wealth, withholding from it the right of Allah. This is the view of al-Ḥasan, from the phrase "so-and-so is shadīd," meaning stingy.

﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered﴾. Concerning it there are three aspects:

The first: those in them of the dead.

The second: its meaning is "died."

The third: it was examined (buḥitha). This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and in the reading of Ibn Masʿūd it is "bu-ḥthira mā fī al-qubūr" (what is in the graves is examined).

﴿And what is in the breasts is obtained﴾. Concerning it there are three aspects:

The first: what is in them is distinguished. This is the view of al-Kalbī.

The second: what is in them is extracted.

The third: what is in them is uncovered.

﴿Indeed, their Lord, that Day, is all-Knowing of them﴾, i.e., aware. It may carry two meanings:

The first: He is aware of what is in their souls.

The second: He is aware of what their affairs will come to.
